summary: An announcement and call for participation for an IEEE Computer Society workshop on Computer Networks at Lake Arrowhead, California, September 8 to 10, 1971. It was aimed at people newly entering the field.

plainLanguage.summary: An invitation to a workshop in the mountains where people who are just starting to work on computer networks can meet and learn.

subtitle: Invitation to a professional workshop for people new to computer networks research.

tldr.problem: The computer networking field was growing rapidly with new sites joining the network, but people new to the field needed a venue to learn from experienced researchers.
tldr.mechanism: The IEEE Computer Society scheduled a three-day workshop at Lake Arrowhead, California on September 8-10, 1971, limited to 65 participants, with sessions on specific network systems, functional capabilities, hardware and software limitations, and network management problems.
tldr.outcome: The workshop brought together active network workers for off-the-record discussion of incomplete and preliminary results, with the goal of stimulating high-quality papers for publication afterward.

today: RFC 169 documents an important professional gathering at the birth of computer networking as a field. The workshop model it describes—off-the-record discussions to generate publishable research—remains a valuable approach to professional conferences today.

sections.title: The Workshop
sections.content:
RFC 169 announces an IEEE Computer Society West Coast workshop on computer networks to be held at Lake Arrowhead, California on September 8-10, 1971. Organized by David Farber (UC Irvine) and Stephen Crocker (ARPA), the workshop was designed especially for people newly entering the networking field, including manufacturers, users and researchers.

Participation was limited to 65 people to encourage discussion, and attendance was by invitation only. The workshop was off-the-record, meaning slides and blackboards could not be photographed and discussions would not be published—allowing participants to discuss preliminary and incomplete results freely.
sections.plainLanguage: In September 1971, computer scientists were invited to a three-day meeting in the mountains. Only 65 people could come. It was secret—no one could publish what was said there.

sections.title: Sessions and Topics
sections.content:
The workshop had four main sessions. Sessions I and II focused on descriptions of specific network systems, their aims, scope, constraints, equipment, protocols and expected lifetime. Session III on functional capabilities covered file transmission, accessing foreign data, remote job entry, resource control and data standards. Session IV addressed limitations of hardware and software, including multiplexers, terminals and network-capable systems.

A panel session on network management problems completed the agenda. Presentations were brief (5-10 minutes) followed by 15-30 minutes of discussion. Participants were encouraged to present preliminary and embryonic systems, not just finished work.
sections.plainLanguage: The four days had talks about different network systems, what jobs they could do, what hardware problems they had, and how to manage a network. Everyone got to argue and ask questions.

sections.title: Philosophy and Goals
sections.content:
The workshop followed IEEE principles for technical gatherings: it brought together active workers in the field for exhaustive discussion of controversial approaches; it used selected mature participants to avoid need for tutorials; it kept discussion focused on a defined topic; and it was limited in size to permit in-depth conversation.

The goal was not to publish proceedings but to stimulate high-quality papers for IEEE meetings afterward. Participants paid a registration fee of $45 covering meals and housing. Invitations were sent around August 15, 1971, for the September meeting.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea was to get smart people in one room to argue about hard problems, and then have them write good papers about what they figured out.
